To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the number of expressed protein-coding transcripts in the human and mouse genomes is much smaller than the number of ESTs, that the number of distinct protein-coding genes that are expressed is much smaller than that of the ESTs, and that the vast majority of the ESTs are not expressed in any tissue.
the vast majority of expressed sequence tags (ESTs) do not code for proteins and that the number of expressed protein-coding genes is approximately 20, 000.

(a) the number of expressed sequences in mammalian genomes greatly surpasses the number of protein-codes genes, (b) only 9%–14% of expressed sequences are able to generate proteins, and (c) the majority of expressed sequences may be redundant, and may represent alternative transcripts of the same protein-coding gene.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the mammalian genome and its expression.
the development and use of computational methods to understand the function of the human genome, with a particular focus on gene structure, alternative splicing and gene evolution.
the development of computational methods for the identification, annotation and classification of genes and gene products in eukaryotic organisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the human genome encodes for approximately 20,500 protein-coding genes, with an error margin of approximately 5% (1000 genes).
ESTs are a valuable tool to identify new protein-coding genes, but that they cannot be used to estimate the number of protein-codes in mammalian genomes.
the number of expressed sequences is approximately 2.5 times the number of protein-codes genes in the human genome.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the number of expressed sequences is not an accurate measure of the number of protein-codes in a genome.
only approximately 20% of the human and mouse genomes are protein coding, which is consistent with the estimate for the human genome.
the vast majority of ESTs are non-coding and that the number of protein-codes in mammals is not much greater than that of the fruitfly.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the majority of ESTs do not code for proteins.
the majority of human-expressed sequences are not protein-coding.
the number of protein-codes in mammalian genomes is much lower than the number of expressed sequences.
